title: The Unsolved Max Headroom Broadcast Intrusion and Its Doctor Who Connection
excerpt:
Two Chicago television signals were interrupted by a masked figure in November 1987.
One intrusion interrupted Doctor Who, and the perpetrators remain unidentified.
body_md:
On the evening of November 22, 1987, Chicago television audiences witnessed one of broadcasting history's most peculiar unsolved incidents. Two stations were interrupted within roughly two hours by a mysterious figure wearing a mask and sunglasses resembling the pop-culture character Max Headroom. The second interruption took place during an episode of Doctor Who, giving the real-life mystery an unexpected connection to science-fiction television.

The first incident occurred at approximately 9:14 p.m. during the sports segment of WGN-TV's evening news. Viewers saw the regular picture disappear briefly before a masked person appeared against a metallic-looking background. The intruder moved erratically, accompanied by static and distorted buzzing rather than intelligible speech. Engineers restored the broadcast after about thirty seconds, leaving sports anchor Dan Roan visibly perplexed.

Roughly two hours later, at around 11:20 p.m., the figure returned on public television station WTTW. This time the interrupted program was Doctor Who, specifically the serial Horror of Fang Rock. The second intrusion included sound, disconnected remarks, pop-culture references and deliberately provocative behavior. It lasted about ninety seconds before the scheduled episode resumed.

The events were not simply studio pranks inserted into the programming. Someone had interfered with the transmission path used to deliver television signals. The Federal Communications Commission investigated, and the FBI became involved. According to the account, the people responsible could have faced a substantial fine, imprisonment, or both if identified and prosecuted.

Investigators never established who was behind the interruptions. Speculation has ranged from disaffected television employees to members of Chicago's underground technical community, but none of these theories has been substantiated. The statute of limitations expired in 1992 without a credible confession, leaving the identity of the perpetrators unknown decades later.

The case has often been compared with the 1986 Captain Midnight incident, when satellite technician John MacDougall interrupted HBO's signal to protest subscription pricing. That earlier perpetrator was identified, unlike the people behind the Max Headroom intrusion. Specialists have suggested the Chicago incident would have required considerable transmission capability and proximity to relevant broadcast facilities.

The transition of American television broadcasting from analog to digital in 2009 changed the technical environment that made this particular kind of interference possible. It would be misleading, however, to suggest that modern digital broadcasting is immune to every form of disruption. Doctor Who's involvement was simply that it happened to be airing when the second interruption occurred; there is no evidence that anyone associated with the series orchestrated the intrusion. That coincidence remains one of the story's most memorable details.
seo_title: Max Headroom's Unsolved 1987 Doctor Who Interruption
seo_description: How a masked intruder interrupted two Chicago broadcasts in 1987, including Doctor Who, and why the Max Headroom case remains unsolved.
